title: How Chocolate Went From 5,300-Year-Old Bean to Bar
description:
The history of chocolate, from cacao beans used 5,300 years ago in the Amazon and the Maya's bitter foamy drink, to Aztec cocoa-bean money, the first chocolate bar in 1847 and the invention of milk chocolate. Plus why chocolate melts in your mouth but not in your hand.

Sources:
https://www.worldhistory.org/Chocolate_in_Mesoamerica/
https://popular-archaeology.com/article/the-indians-of-the-ecuadorian-amazon-were-using-cocoa-5300-years-ago/
https://cocoarunners.com/2022/07/an-industrial-history-of-chocolate/

Animated in the Claymation Set style.

topic: The Story of Chocolate: How It All Started
script: You could buy a turkey with a hundred cocoa beans. So why did chocolate stop being money, and how did it end up in your hand? This is the story of chocolate. It starts with a tree in the rainforest. The cacao tree grows big, football-shaped pods, right on its trunk. Inside each pod are thirty to fifty seeds, wrapped in sweet white pulp. Those seeds are cocoa beans. Scientists found traces of cacao in pots from the Amazon in Ecuador, about five thousand three hundred years old. Later, the Olmec and the Maya turned the beans into a drink. They roasted them, ground them into paste, and mixed in water, chili, and cornmeal. Then they poured it from high up, from one cup into another, to whip up a thick foam on top. And here's the thing. It wasn't sweet at all. It was bitter, spicy, and very special. The Aztecs loved it so much they used the beans as money. One record from the fifteen hundreds lists prices. A tomato cost one bean. An avocado, three beans. A turkey hen, one hundred. Some people even made fake beans, by stuffing empty shells with mud. Then, in the fifteen hundreds, Spanish explorers carried cacao back across the ocean. The Spanish court tried the bitter drink, and did something new. They added sugar, plus cinnamon and vanilla. Suddenly, Europe was hooked. Fancy chocolate houses opened in London, where rich people sipped it hot. But for almost three hundred years, chocolate was still only a drink. Here's why. A cocoa bean is about half fat, called cocoa butter. Grind the beans, and you get a thick, greasy paste. In eighteen twenty eight, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten built a press that squeezed out most of that butter. What was left became a dry cake, that could be crushed into cocoa powder. Then in eighteen forty seven, an English company called Fry's flipped the idea. They mixed cocoa powder and sugar with extra melted cocoa butter, and poured it into a mold. It set hard. The first modern chocolate bar. It was still gritty, and a bit bitter. Two Swiss makers fixed that. In eighteen seventy five, Daniel Peter added milk, using milk powder from his neighbor, Henri Nestlé. Milk chocolate was born. Then in eighteen seventy nine, Rodolphe Lindt built a machine called a conche. It rolls warm chocolate back and forth for hours, grinding every bit smaller and smaller, until it turns silky smooth. So what happens today? Farmers cut open the pods and let the beans ferment for about a week. That's where most of the chocolate flavor comes from. Then the beans are dried, roasted, and cracked. It takes around four hundred beans to make one pound of chocolate. And the best trick is in the butter. Cocoa butter melts at about thirty four degrees Celsius, just below the heat inside your mouth. That's why a bar stays solid in your hand, but melts on your tongue. From a bitter drink worth real money, to the bar in your lunchbox. So, would you rather have the drink, or the bar? Next time, how do tiny ants build an underground city for millions of workers?
key_facts: Traces of cacao in ~5,300-year-old pottery from the Ecuadorian Amazon (2018 study)
Olmec and Maya drank cacao as a bitter, foamy drink with chili and cornmeal
Aztecs used cacao beans as money; a 1545 list: tomato 1 bean, avocado 3, turkey hen 100
Spanish added sugar, cinnamon and vanilla; London chocolate houses from 1657
1828 van Houten press separates cocoa butter; 1847 Fry's first solid bar
1875 Daniel Peter milk chocolate with Nestle's milk; 1879 Lindt's conche
~400 beans per pound of chocolate; cocoa butter melts ~34 C, below mouth temperature
